rationale: A wins because it knows where the facts stop. Its headline, "Instacart's ad business hit a $1B run rate while its core delivery growth fell to single digits," is the clean tension in the update; B's "Instacart's delivery growth has stalled" turns slow growth into no growth, and "Why 1,500 grocery banners are renting their tech stack" stretches a partnership count into an outsourcing thesis. B is sharper in places, but clever overreach is still overreach.
gaps_in_A: The first two angles both lean on the ad-business facts; A keeps them distinct by altitude, but the ad-trade angle needs real benchmarks or it collapses into the contrarian markets angle.
"Caper smart carts let shoppers skip the checkout line — and they're spreading to more chains" is close to product-rollout copy until named chains and operational results show up.
A misses an explicit guardrail B caught: the supplied facts do not say ads run on Caper carts.
gaps_in_B: "Instacart's delivery growth has stalled" is too strong; the update says order growth slowed to single digits, not stopped.
"Why 1,500 grocery banners are renting their tech stack instead of building it" invents a rental/outsourcing frame from a generic partnership count.
"slowing core, accelerating adjacency" claims acceleration the update never gives; a $1B run rate is scale, not a growth rate.
"The checkout line is quietly disappearing from a few hundred grocery stores" overstates the rollout; smart carts are live in stores, not necessarily replacing checkout lines storewide.
